Name: ambiguity_specification_gap
Title: Precision or Pragmatics? Measuring How Natural Language Underspecification Shapes and Bottlenecks LLM Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: Natural language is systematically underspecified—it relies on the reader's pragmatic inference to fill semantic gaps (scope ambiguity, vague quantifiers, unresolved reference, implicit presuppositions). We hypothesize that (a) a large fraction of LLM reasoning failures on ordinary word problems are caused not by faulty reasoning but by silent, incorrect resolution of these underspecifications; (b) a per-problem 'specification gap' (the number/type of latent interpretive choices) predicts failure; and (c) causally precisifying the language (making the intended interpretation explicit) recovers most lost accuracy, while precisifying to an UNINTENDED-but-valid reading changes the answer in a way that reveals the model was reasoning correctly over the wrong interpretation.
Related Work: Prior work on ambiguity in LLMs (e.g., AmbigQA, task/instruction ambiguity, clarification-question agents like ReSpAct) studies whether models detect ambiguity or ask for clarification, and reasoning-failure surveys (Song et al. 2026) catalog error types without isolating interpretation errors. Robustness work on paraphrase/perturbation sensitivity shows accuracy varies with surface form but does not attribute variance to specific interpretive choices. My own prior proposals concern typology, linguistic content, naming, pivot language, dialects, narrative order, obligatory marking, and structural transfer—none address SEMANTIC UNDERSPECIFICATION as a reasoning bottleneck. This proposal is distinct: it formalizes a per-problem specification gap over enumerable interpretive dimensions, causally tests precisification-to-intended vs precisification-to-alternative readings, and separates 'wrong interpretation' errors from 'wrong reasoning' errors—re-scoring reasoning ability once interpretation is controlled.
Abstract: Natural language leaves much unsaid, delegating disambiguation to the reader's pragmatic inference. When an LLM solves a word problem, it must silently resolve scope ambiguities, vague quantifiers ('a few', 'most'), unresolved pronoun/definite reference, and implicit presuppositions before it can reason. We ask how much of what looks like faulty LLM reasoning is actually correct reasoning over a silently mis-chosen interpretation. We construct reasoning problems (arithmetic word problems, temporal/scheduling puzzles, and logic/reference puzzles) annotated with an enumerable set of latent interpretive choice points, giving each problem a 'specification gap' score and a set of valid alternative readings. For each problem we produce: the original underspecified form; a precisified-to-intended form (making the canonical interpretation explicit, holding content otherwise fixed); and precisified-to-alternative forms (each a different valid reading). Using open models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2), we test whether the specification gap predicts final-answer failure via mixed-effects regression controlling for length and difficulty, and whether precisify-to-intended causally recovers accuracy. Crucially, for original-form errors we check whether the produced answer matches an alternative-reading solution—quantifying an 'interpretation-error rate' distinct from a 'reasoning-error rate.' We further probe whether models can, on demand, enumerate the interpretations and whether self-precisification (asking the model to disambiguate before solving) helps. Results would re-partition LLM reasoning ability into interpretation and computation components, reframe many benchmark errors as pragmatic mis-resolution, and clarify how language's tolerance for underspecification both enables and bottlenecks machine reasoning.
Experiments: 1) DATASET WITH ANNOTATED INTERPRETIVE CHOICE POINTS (~450 problems across 3 families): (a) arithmetic/quantity word problems containing vague quantifiers or ambiguous grouping/scope; (b) temporal/scheduling problems with ambiguous relative-time or ordering references; (c) reference/logic puzzles with unresolved pronouns or definite descriptions. For each problem, annotate an enumerable set of interpretive choice points and the resulting valid alternative readings, each with a computed correct answer via an automatic solver. Define SpecificationGap = number (and weighted type) of latent choice points. 2) PRECISIFICATION VARIANTS: for each problem generate (i) ORIGINAL underspecified text; (ii) PRECISIFY-INTENDED (canonical reading made explicit, content otherwise held fixed, verified equivalent); (iii) PRECISIFY-ALT_k (each valid alternative reading made explicit). Validate fluency and that only the interpretive dimension changed via automated checks and human spot-checks. 3) MAIN PREDICTION: for each model (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B) solve ORIGINAL problems; fit mixed-effects logistic regression correct ~ SpecificationGap + log(#tokens) + difficulty + (1|problem) + (1|model); report coefficient, effect size, per-model AUC of SpecificationGap as a failure predictor. 4) CAUSAL PRECISIFICATION: compare accuracy on PRECISIFY-INTENDED vs ORIGINAL; report % of the original-form gap recovered. Predict large recovery if failures are interpretive. 5) INTERPRETATION- vs REASONING-ERROR DECOMPOSITION: for every ORIGINAL error, check whether the model's answer equals the correct solution under any valid ALTERNATIVE reading. Label as INTERPRETATION-ERROR (matches an alternative) vs REASONING-ERROR (matches none). Report the split per family/model—this re-partitions measured 'reasoning failure.' Corroborate by running PRECISIFY-ALT_k and checking the model then produces that reading's answer (consistency of the interpretation hypothesis). 6) SELF-PRECISIFICATION: prompt the model to first enumerate possible interpretations and state its chosen reading, then solve; measure (a) accuracy change vs original, (b) whether its stated reading matches its answer, and (c) recall of annotated interpretations (enumeration coverage). 7) GENERALIZATION/SCALING: test consistency across families and two model sizes; report interaction between SpecificationGap and family. METRICS: accuracy, SpecificationGap regression coefficient/AUC, precisify-intended recovery %, interpretation-error vs reasoning-error rates, alternative-reading answer-match rate, interpretation enumeration recall, self-precisification accuracy delta; all with mixed-effects models and CIs.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Enumerating ALL valid interpretations is only tractable for constructed/structured problems; naturalistic text may have open-ended ambiguity—mitigated by using generators with known choice points and reporting per-family differences. 2) Precisification edits may subtly alter difficulty or fluency; mitigated by holding content fixed except the target dimension and validating with automated equivalence and human spot-checks. 3) An answer matching an alternative reading could be coincidental (multiple readings yield the same number); we design alternatives to yield distinct answers where possible and report the ambiguity-of-match rate. 4) Self-precisification adds tokens/serial compute, confounding with extra computation; addressed with a token-matched 'restate the problem' control. 5) Effects may be model- or scale-specific; multiple models/sizes and effect-size reporting address this. 6) A finding that precisification barely helps would still be informative—indicating failures are genuine reasoning errors rather than interpretive ones, which itself sharpens the language–intelligence question.
